props.title: 10 Rillington Place
props.initialSlug: Chilling true story of a mild-mannered serial killer

sections.content: 10 Rillington Place (1971) stands as one of the most chilling true-crime films ever made, with Richard Attenborough delivering an unnervingly subtle performance as serial killer John Christie. Like In Cold Blood (1967) and Compulsion (1959), it pioneered the meticulous true-crime drama format that would later influence films like Zodiac (2007). Director Richard Fleischer crafts a suffocating atmosphere in the cramped London flat where Christie committed his murders, using claustrophobic framing and muted colors to enhance the psychological horror.

sections.content: The film's power lies in its unflinching examination of institutional failure and social inequality in post-war Britain. Like Dance with a Stranger (1985) and Let Him Have It (1991), it exposes how class prejudice and systemic incompetence led to tragic miscarriages of justice. The wrongful execution of Timothy Evans, portrayed with devastating effect by John Hurt, becomes a damning indictment of capital punishment.

Attenborough's portrayal of Christie revolutionized how serial killers were depicted on screen. Instead of a obvious monster, he plays Christie as an outwardly respectable member of society - a former special constable who uses his air of authority to gain trust. This influenced later performances like Anthony Hopkins in The Silence of the Lambs (1991) and Brian Cox in Manhunter (1986). SUBHEAD: Impact on True Crime Cinema

sections.content: The film's documentary-like approach, shooting in actual locations including the real Rillington Place, set a template for authentic true crime storytelling that influenced works like Summer of Sam (1999) and Monster (2003). Its unflinching examination of social issues through the lens of true crime paved the way for films like The Thin Blue Line (1988) and Paradise Lost (1996).
